title: Men and women for others
hook: Arrupe's phrase for what Jesuit education should form

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pedro Arrupe at Hiroshima. Your line was he turned the house into a hospital. Where did you find a way to open your door a little wider? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-eight.
screen: `HE TURNED THE HOUSE INTO A HOSPITAL.`

segments.voice: A room full of former students of Jesuit schools, gathered in Spain. Doctors, lawyers, business owners, comfortable people, proud of their schooling. The man at the podium is the same Pedro Arrupe from yesterday, now the head of the whole Jesuit order. They might expect a warm speech about the old days. Instead he asks a hard question: have Jesuit schools taught you to care about justice, or only to succeed? Then he offers a short phrase for what those schools are supposed to produce. Tradition says some in the room did not like it. The phrase stayed anyway. Today's word.
screen: `FORMER STUDENTS, COMFORTABLE, PROUD.` → `HAVE WE TAUGHT YOU JUSTICE?` → `A PHRASE SOME DIDN'T LIKE.`

segments.voice: Men and women for others. In Arrupe's own Spanish the talk was called hombres para los demás, men for others. He said the aim of Jesuit education should be to form people who live not for themselves but for God and for others, especially the poor. And he said something harder: that the schools had sometimes failed at it, and that he was asking forgiveness for that. In time, as Jesuit schools welcomed girls and women, the phrase grew into men and women for others, and that's the form you'll hear now. What makes it more than a slogan? Three things. First, it's about who you become, not only what you do. Volunteering on a Saturday is good; Arrupe was asking about the shape of a whole life. Second, it includes justice, not just charity. He wanted people to ask why someone is hungry, not only to hand them bread. Third, it's rooted in Jesus himself. In Mark's Gospel, in the Douay-Rheims, Jesus says the Son of man "is not come to be ministered unto: but to minister." Served, or serving: the phrase picks a side. Here's the honest part. For others can curdle into self-importance, the helper who needs to be needed. The Ignatian answer is the examen: look back each night and ask who the day was really for. In practice, for others might be as plain as letting someone go ahead in line, or as big as rethinking what your job is for.
screen: `HOMBRES PARA LOS DEMÁS.` · `WHO YOU BECOME, NOT ONLY WHAT YOU DO.` · `JUSTICE, NOT ONLY CHARITY.` · `WHO WAS THE DAY REALLY FOR?` · then, large: `NOT TO BE MINISTERED UNTO, BUT TO MINISTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one thing for others. Settle, and breathe. Look ahead at the rest of today or tomorrow. Where is one place you could do something for someone else that they didn't ask for and won't pay you back for? Make it concrete: a name, a task, a time. Then ask the second question, the justice one: is there anything behind their need that you could learn about, or speak up about? If you pray, you can offer the plan to God and ask for a clear heart in doing it. The bell holds the time.
Men and women for others. Pedro Arrupe's phrase for what Jesuit education should form: people who live for God and others, with justice, not only charity. Today's word.
screen: `MEN AND WOMEN FOR OTHERS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: for others. Today, do the thing you planned, and tonight ask who it was really for. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-eight.
